source.text: Καὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μαρτυρία τοῦ Ἰωάννου ὅτε ἀπέστειλαν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἐξ Ἱεροσολύμων ἱερεῖς καὶ Λευίτας ἵνα ἐρωτήσωσιν αὐτόν· Σὺ τίς εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: And this is the testimony of the John, when sent the Jews out of Jerusalem priests and Levites so that they might ask him, "You, who are you?"

en.L: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent out from Jerusalem priests and Levites in order that they might ask him, "You, who are you?"
en.B: This is what John testified when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?"
en.R: This is what John said when the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites, who served in the temple, to ask him, "Who are you?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: here the religious authorities in Jerusalem
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: John uses this word in several senses: the Jewish people (4:9, 22), people of Judea (11:19), and often the religious authorities in Jerusalem. Here they send priests and Levites from Jerusalem with official questions, and the envoys must report back to those who sent them (verse 22); verse 24 links the delegation with the Pharisees. That is the leadership, not the whole people. John the Baptist, Jesus and his first disciples are all Jews.

decisions.choice: priests and Levites: officials of the Jerusalem temple
decisions.reason: Priests offered the sacrifices in the temple. Levites, from the same tribe of Levi, assisted them and kept order there. Sending them makes this an official inquiry into who John claims to be.

decisions.choice: testimony: John's formal witness, picking up 1:7-8 and 1:15
decisions.reason: The opening said John came to testify about the light (1:7). What follows, up to 1:34, is that testimony: first what John says about himself (1:19-28), then what he says about Jesus (1:29-34). The word has the sense of evidence given before a court.

decisions.choice: emphatic you: "You, who are you?"
decisions.reason: Σὺ stands first in the question. The envoys press John to say who he himself claims to be.

decisions.choice: the Jews (L); the Jewish leaders (B); the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: Literal shows the word John wrote; Balanced and Readable name the group the context shows (meaning decision m1), so no reader takes it as the whole Jewish people.

decisions.choice: who served in the temple
decisions.reason: Readable says who the Levites were (meaning decision m2).

source.text: καὶ ὡμολόγησεν καὶ οὐκ ἠρνήσατο, καὶ ὡμολόγησεν ὅτι Ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ὁ χριστός.

records.literal_gloss: And he confessed and not denied, and confessed that "I not am the Christ."

en.L: And he declared openly, and did not deny [it], and declared openly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."
en.B: He spoke openly and did not refuse to answer; he stated plainly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."
en.R: John did not hide anything. He told them clearly, "I am not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."

decisions.choice: declared openly, as one does in public or before a court
decisions.reason: ὁμολογέω means to say something openly or acknowledge it publicly; it is not admitting a sin here. Saying it, denying the opposite, and saying it again stresses how plainly John answered.

decisions.choice: did not deny: did not evade the question
alternatives: did not deny that he was the Christ
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. Placed between the two positive statements, it means John did not refuse to answer or hide behind vague words.

decisions.choice: emphatic I: I am not the Christ (someone else is)
decisions.reason: Ἐγὼ is emphatic. The envoys asked only who he was, but John answers the question behind it (compare Luke 3:15, where people wondered whether John was the Christ). The emphasis prepares for verses 26-27: he is not the one, but the one is already among them.

decisions.choice: the Christ: a title, the Anointed One, the king Israel was waiting for
decisions.reason: With the article, χριστός is a title here, not a name. 1:41 gives the Hebrew word, Messiah, which means the same.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Here the word is a title with the article, so every level writes "the" outside the span: "the Christ" or "the Messiah". The usual Balanced span would give "I am not Christ", which reads as a name.

decisions.choice: did not refuse to answer (B); did not hide anything (R)
decisions.reason: English "deny" needs an object; these say what meaning decision m2 finds.

source.text: καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτόν· Τί οὖν;

records.literal_gloss: And they asked him, "What then?

en.L: And they asked him, "What then?
en.B: So they asked him, "Then what?
en.R: They asked him, "Then who are you?

decisions.choice: What then?: if not the Christ, what are you?
decisions.reason: Τί οὖν is a short follow-up: if you are not the Christ, what is the answer? The exchange moves quickly, in short questions and shorter answers.

decisions.choice: who
decisions.reason: In English one asks "who" about a person; the sense is the same.

source.text: σὺ Ἠλίας εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: You Elijah are?

en.L: Are you Elijah?"
en.B: Are you Elijah?"
en.R: Are you Elijah?"

decisions.choice: Elijah, whose return Malachi promised
decisions.reason: Malachi 4:5-6 (3:23-24 in the Hebrew numbering) says God will send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD. Elijah had been taken up alive (2 Kings 2:11), and he was expected to come back. John dressed as Elijah had (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6), so the question was a natural one.

source.text: καὶ λέγει· Οὐκ εἰμί.

records.literal_gloss: And he says, "Not I am."

en.L: And he says, "I am not."
en.B: He said, "I am not."
en.R: "No, I am not," he said.

decisions.choice: John denies being Elijah himself come back
alternatives: John denies any link with Elijah
decisions.reason: Jesus says that John is the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14; 17:12-13), and Luke 1:17 says John would go ahead of the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. John is not denying that role. He denies being Elijah himself returned, which is what he was asked; in this Gospel John always points away from himself to Jesus (3:30).

decisions.choice: past tense: he said
decisions.reason: John often tells his story in the present tense ("he says", "he finds"), which makes it vivid. Literal keeps it; Balanced and Readable use the past, as English stories do. This applies throughout the passage.

source.text: Ὁ προφήτης εἶ σύ;

records.literal_gloss: The prophet are you?

en.L: "Are you the Prophet?"
en.B: "Are you the Prophet?"
en.R: "Are you the Prophet that Moses promised?"

decisions.choice: the Prophet: the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-18
alternatives: one of the old prophets come back
decisions.reason: The article points to a known figure. God told Moses he would raise up a prophet like him from among the people (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18). Later in John people wonder whether Jesus is "the Prophet" (6:14; 7:40), and Peter applies the promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22). Here, as in 7:40-41, the Prophet is treated as someone other than the Christ.

decisions.choice: the Prophet, with a capital
decisions.reason: The capital shows a particular, expected figure (meaning decision m1), not any prophet.

decisions.choice: that Moses promised
decisions.reason: Readable says which prophet is meant (meaning decision m1).

source.text: καὶ ἀπεκρίθη· Οὔ.

records.literal_gloss: And he answered, "No."

en.L: And he answered, "No."
en.B: He answered, "No."
en.R: "No," he answered.

decisions.choice: John's answers grow shorter
decisions.reason: "I am not the Christ", then "I am not", and now a single word. The story shows John stepping out of the way.

source.text: εἶπαν οὖν αὐτῷ· Τίς εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: They said therefore to him, "Who are you?

en.L: So they said to him, "Who are you?
en.B: So they said to him, "Who are you, then?
en.R: So they said, "Who are you?

decisions.choice: so: the question follows from his three denials
decisions.reason: οὖν links the question to what John has said: if he is none of these, who is he? It brings the envoys back to their first question (verse 19).

source.text: ἵνα ἀπόκρισιν δῶμεν τοῖς πέμψασιν ἡμᾶς· τί λέγεις περὶ σεαυτοῦ;

records.literal_gloss: So that an answer we may give to the [ones] having sent us; what do you say about yourself?"

en.L: [Tell us,] so that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
en.B: We have to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"
en.R: We have to take an answer back to the leaders who sent us. What do you say about yourself?"

decisions.choice: a purpose clause with its main verb unstated: [tell us] so that
decisions.reason: ἵνα begins a clause of purpose with nothing before it to depend on. The sense is "tell us, so that": the envoys must report back.

decisions.choice: those who sent us: the authorities of verse 19
decisions.reason: The envoys are not asking for themselves; they speak for the leaders in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: [Tell us,]
decisions.reason: English cannot begin a sentence with "so that" alone (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: We have to give an answer ...
alternatives: so that we may give an answer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the purpose clause into a plain statement of need; Readable names the leaders (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἔφη· Ἐγὼ φωνὴ βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ· Εὐθύνατε τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίου, καθὼς εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας ὁ προφήτης.

records.literal_gloss: He said, "I [am] a voice of [one] crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of Lord,' as said Isaiah the prophet."

en.L: He said, "I [am] a voice of [one] crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of [the] Lord,' as Isaiah the prophet said."
en.B: John answered in the words of the prophet Isaiah: "I am a voice of someone calling out in the wilderness, 'Make the road straight for the Lord.'"
en.R: John said, "I am the voice that the prophet Isaiah spoke about. Someone is shouting in the desert, 'Make a straight road for the Lord!'"

decisions.choice: John's words quote Isaiah 40:3
decisions.reason: Isaiah 40 opens God's message of comfort to his people in exile: the LORD himself is coming back to them, and a voice calls for a road to be made ready for him through the wilderness. John takes that voice as his own role. He is only a voice; what matters is the one who is coming. Isaiah's Greek has two verbs, "prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths"; John's words join them into one. Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3 and Luke 3:4 apply the same verse to John.

decisions.choice: Lord: in Isaiah 40:3 this stands for God's own name, the LORD
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 40:3 the word is the divine name. John prepares the way for Jesus, so the Gospel applies to Jesus a verse about the coming of the LORD himself (compare 1:1, 14).

decisions.choice: "as Isaiah the prophet said" is part of John's answer
decisions.reason: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the narrator introduces the quotation. Here the words continue John's reply: he himself names Isaiah as his source.

decisions.choice: Isaiah named before the quotation
alternatives: as Isaiah the prophet said (at the end)
decisions.reason: After a quotation inside a quotation, a closing "as Isaiah the prophet said" is hard to follow in English. Balanced and Readable name Isaiah first; Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here the Gospel quotes the verse with the Greek word "Lord"; meaning decision m2 explains whom it means.

decisions.choice: desert
decisions.reason: The word means empty country where few people live, such as the dry land along the lower Jordan. "Desert" is the everyday word for it.

source.text: Καὶ ἀπεσταλμένοι ἦσαν ἐκ τῶν Φαρισαίων.

records.literal_gloss: And [ones] having been sent were from the Pharisees.

en.L: And they had been sent from the Pharisees.
en.B: They had been sent by the Pharisees.
en.R: The Pharisees had sent them.

decisions.choice: the envoys had been sent on behalf of the Pharisees
alternatives: some Pharisees had also been sent: a second group, or members of the same group
decisions.reason: ἐκ with "the Pharisees" can mean "from" a group as the senders, or "some of" the group (as in 1:35, "two of his disciples"). Verse 19 has just named the senders as the leaders in Jerusalem, and this verse adds that the Pharisees were behind the questions. But the Greek can also say that some Pharisees had been sent, perhaps as a further delegation that asks the question in verse 25. Literal keeps the open wording; a footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: no article before "sent" (SBLGNT)
alternatives: with the article: those who had been sent were from the Pharisees (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add the article, which makes the verse say that the same envoys came from the Pharisees. The older reading leaves it more open (meaning decision m1). The difference is small, so no separate footnote.

decisions.choice: Pharisees: a movement devoted to keeping the law exactly
decisions.reason: The Pharisees were a group within Judaism known for careful keeping of the law of Moses and the traditions that explained it, and they had wide influence among the people. In John they question Jesus often (7:32; 9:13-16).

source.text: καὶ ἠρώτησαν αὐτὸν καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Τί οὖν βαπτίζεις εἰ σὺ οὐκ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς οὐδὲ Ἠλίας οὐδὲ ὁ προφήτης;

records.literal_gloss: And they asked him and said to him, "Why then do you baptize if you not are the Christ nor Elijah nor the prophet?"

en.L: And they asked him and said to him, "Why then do you baptize, if you are not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?"
en.B: They questioned him further: "Why are you baptizing, then, if you are not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, or Elijah, or the Prophet?"
en.R: They asked him, "You are not the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, or Elijah, or the Prophet. So why are you baptizing people?"

decisions.choice: baptizing: immersing others in water as a sign of turning back to God
decisions.reason: βαπτίζω means to dip or immerse. Jews washed themselves to be ritually clean, but John immersed other people, calling Israel to turn back to God before the coming one arrived. The envoys assume that such an act needs authority from one of the figures God had promised; the prophets had spoken of God cleansing his people with water in the coming age (Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1).

decisions.choice: asked and said: two verbs for one question
decisions.reason: "Asked him and said to him" is a Hebrew way of introducing speech. It is one question, not two.

decisions.choice: the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 20: a title with the article.

decisions.choice: the three denials first, then the question
decisions.reason: Readable states what John has said he is not, then asks the question, in two short sentences.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰωάννης λέγων· Ἐγὼ βαπτίζω ἐν ὕδατι· μέσος ὑμῶν ἕστηκεν ὃν ὑμεῖς οὐκ οἴδατε, ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος, οὗ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἄξιος ἵνα λύσω αὐτοῦ τὸν ἱμάντα τοῦ ὑποδήματος.

records.literal_gloss: Answered them the John saying, "I baptize in water; in midst of you stands [one] whom you not know, \v 27 the [one] after me coming, of whom not I am worthy that I should untie his the strap of the sandal."

en.L: John answered them, saying, "I baptize in water; among you stands [one] whom you do not know, \v 27 the one coming after me, of whom I am not worthy that I should untie {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sandal strap."
en.B: John answered them, "I baptize with water. But someone stands among you whom you do not know. \v 27 He is the one who comes after me, and I am not worthy even to untie the strap of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sandal."
en.R: John answered, "I baptize people with water. But someone is standing here among you, and you do not know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. \v 27 He is coming after me. I am not good enough even to untie {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} sandals, which was a slave's job."

decisions.choice: in water or with water: the water John immerses people in
decisions.reason: ἐν can name the element ("in water") or the means ("with water"); both describe the same act. The phrase is set against baptizing "in the Holy Spirit" in verse 33: John's washing is outward, and the one coming gives the Spirit.

decisions.choice: two statements side by side: I baptize; but among you stands one
decisions.reason: The second statement is John's real answer to "why do you baptize?": his baptism points to someone already present and not yet recognized (compare 1:10, the world did not know him). The perfect ἕστηκεν pictures him as having taken his place among them.

decisions.choice: the one coming after me: later in time, as in 1:15 and 1:30
decisions.reason: ὀπίσω can describe a disciple walking behind a teacher, but here, as in 1:15 and 1:30, it is the one who comes after John in time and ranks above him.

decisions.choice: untying sandals was a slave's task
decisions.reason: Sandals were tied on with leather straps. Untying and removing a master's sandals, and washing his feet, was the work of a slave (compare 13:4-14). John ranks himself below a slave beside the one who is coming.

decisions.choice: in water (L); with water (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the preposition's basic sense; Balanced and Readable use the usual English phrase (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Christ uses the deity_pronoun setting; at the start of a sentence "He" is written plain.

decisions.choice: which was a slave's job
decisions.reason: Readable says why untying sandals was so low a task (meaning decision m4).

source.text: ταῦτα ἐν Βηθανίᾳ ἐγένετο πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων.

records.literal_gloss: These things in Bethany took place across the Jordan, where was the John baptizing.

en.L: These things happened in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
en.B: All this happened at Bethany on the east side of the Jordan River, where John was baptizing.
en.R: All this happened at a place called Bethany, on the east side of the Jordan River. John was baptizing people there.

decisions.choice: Bethany (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read Bethany. Origen, in the early 200s, could not find a Bethany by the Jordan and preferred Bethabara, a reading found in many later manuscripts and in the King James Version. A footnote gives it. Reviewers should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a Bethany east of the Jordan, not the village near Jerusalem
decisions.reason: John 11:18 places another Bethany, the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, near Jerusalem. "Beyond the Jordan" marks this one as east of the river, as seen from Judea; its exact site is not known for certain. Jesus returns there in 10:40.

decisions.choice: on the east side of the Jordan River
decisions.reason: Says plainly what "beyond" means from Judea, and that the Jordan is a river (meaning decision m2).

source.text: Τῇ ἐπαύριον βλέπει τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐρχόμενον πρὸς αὐτόν, καὶ λέγει· Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου.

records.literal_gloss: On the next day he sees the Jesus coming toward him, and says, "Look, the lamb of the God, the [one] taking away the sin of the world.

en.L: On the next day he sees Jesus coming toward him, and says, "Look, the Lamb of God, the one taking away the sin of the world!
en.B: The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, "Look, there is the Lamb of God, who carries away the sin of the world!
en.R: The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him. John said, "Look! There is the Lamb of God, who takes the world's sin away!

decisions.choice: the Lamb of God: the lamb God provides as a sacrifice for sin; the Passover lamb and the lamb of Isaiah 53 are both in view
alternatives: a conquering leader, as the Lamb is pictured in Revelation
decisions.reason: Several Old Testament pictures meet here. In Genesis 22:8 Abraham tells Isaac that God will provide the lamb. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb protected Israel (Exodus 12); John later places Jesus's death on the day the Passover lambs were killed (19:14) and applies to him the rule that none of the lamb's bones may be broken (19:36; Exodus 12:46). Isaiah 53:7 compares the LORD's servant to a lamb led to the slaughter, and says he bore the sin of many (53:12). Lambs were also offered every morning and evening in the temple (Exodus 29:38-42). John does not choose between these, and the translation keeps the title as he gives it. A footnote gives the background.

decisions.choice: takes away: lifts sin up and carries it off
decisions.reason: αἴρω means to lift up and carry away; here it includes both carrying sin and removing it. The present participle describes what he does, his work, rather than one moment.

decisions.choice: sin, singular: the world's sin as a whole
decisions.reason: John speaks of the sin of the world as one great burden, not a list of wrongs.

decisions.choice: world: humanity, all people
decisions.reason: Key term. Here κόσμου means humanity as a whole, cut off from God by its sin; the Lamb is for the whole world, not Israel alone (compare 3:16-17; 4:42).

decisions.choice: John saw ... said
decisions.reason: Past tense, as in verse 21; Balanced and Readable name John, since "he" could be taken as Jesus.

decisions.choice: Look
decisions.reason: Ἴδε calls attention: "look, here is". The style guide does not use "behold".

decisions.choice: carries away (B); takes ... away (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced's "carries away" keeps both parts of the verb (meaning decision m2); Readable uses the simplest words.

source.text: οὗτός ἐστιν ὑπὲρ οὗ ἐγὼ εἶπον· Ὀπίσω μου ἔρχεται ἀνὴρ ὃς ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονεν, ὅτι πρῶτός μου ἦν·

records.literal_gloss: This is [he] concerning whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ahead of me has become, because first of me he was.'

en.L: This is [the one] concerning whom I said, 'After me comes a man who has come to be ahead of me, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was before me.'
en.B: This is the one I meant when I said, 'A man who comes after me ranks ahead of me, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} existed before me.'
en.R: He is the one I was talking about when I said, 'A man is coming after me who is greater than I am, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} existed before me.'

decisions.choice: John repeats his words of 1:15
decisions.reason: John quotes himself, as verse 15 already did, with the same two contrasts: ahead of me in rank, and before me in existence (see the meaning decisions at 1:15).

decisions.choice: a man: a male person, Jesus
decisions.reason: ἀνὴρ is the word for a man as distinct from a woman, and it refers to Jesus, so the gender setting does not apply.

decisions.choice: ranks ahead of me / is greater than I am; existed before me
alternatives: has come to be ahead of me; was before me
decisions.reason: The same wording as 1:15, so readers can see that John is repeating himself.

source.text: κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτόν, ἀλλ’ ἵνα φανερωθῇ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ διὰ τοῦτο ἦλθον ἐγὼ ἐν ὕδατι βαπτίζων.

records.literal_gloss: And I not knew him, but so that he might be revealed to the Israel, because of this came I in water baptizing.

en.L: And I did not know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, but so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water."
en.B: I myself did not know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, but I came baptizing with water so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might be revealed to Israel."
en.R: I myself did not know who {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was. But I came and baptized people with water so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could be shown to the people of Israel."

decisions.choice: did not know him: did not know that he was the one
decisions.reason: Luke 1:36 makes John and Jesus relatives, so John may have known him as a person. What John did not know, until God gave him the sign (verse 33), was that Jesus was the coming one. κἀγὼ ("and I") is emphatic: John's not knowing is set against God's revealing.

decisions.choice: the purpose of John's baptism: that Jesus be revealed to Israel
decisions.reason: The purpose clause comes before the main verb for emphasis: this is why John came baptizing. φανερόω, to make visible, is one of John's words for Jesus showing who he is (2:11; 21:1).

decisions.choice: I came baptizing ... so that he might be revealed
alternatives: so that he might be revealed ... for this reason I came
decisions.reason: English puts the purpose after the main clause; Literal keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Israel here is the people, not the land.

source.text: καὶ ἐμαρτύρησεν Ἰωάννης λέγων ὅτι Τεθέαμαι τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον ὡς περιστερὰν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ ἔμεινεν ἐπ’ αὐτόν·

records.literal_gloss: And testified John saying that "I have beheld the Spirit coming down as a dove out of heaven, and [it] remained upon him;

en.L: And John testified, saying, "I have seen the Spirit coming down as a dove out of heaven, and [the Spirit] remained on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: John also gave this testimony: "I saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.R: John said, "I saw the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the Spirit: the Holy Spirit
decisions.reason: Verse 33 names him the Holy Spirit.

decisions.choice: as a dove: the Spirit came down in a visible form like a dove
alternatives: the Spirit came down the way a dove flies down
decisions.reason: ὡς can compare the form or the manner. Luke 3:22 says the Spirit came down "in bodily form, like a dove", which supports a visible form; John says no more than that he saw it.

decisions.choice: remained: the Spirit stayed on him, not just a passing visit
decisions.reason: μένω, "remain", is one of John's key words. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on prophets and leaders for a task; on Jesus the Spirit remains, and verse 33 makes this the sign God gave. Isaiah 11:2 says the Spirit of the LORD will rest on the king from David's line, and Isaiah 42:1 that God will put his Spirit on his chosen servant (compare verse 34). The same verb returns in verses 38-39.

decisions.choice: I saw
decisions.reason: The Greek perfect presents what John saw as standing evidence; English narrative uses the simple past. Literal keeps "I have seen".

decisions.choice: [the Spirit] remained (L); remain (B, R)
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject, and the word for Spirit is neuter in Greek, which says nothing about whether the Spirit is a person. English repeats "the Spirit" or joins the verbs, rather than calling the Spirit "it".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to Jesus.

source.text: κἀγὼ οὐκ ᾔδειν αὐτόν, ἀλλ’ ὁ πέμψας με βαπτίζειν ἐν ὕδατι ἐκεῖνός μοι εἶπεν· Ἐφ’ ὃν ἂν ἴδῃς τὸ πνεῦμα καταβαῖνον καὶ μένον ἐπ’ αὐτόν, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ βαπτίζων ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ·

records.literal_gloss: And I not knew him, but the [one] having sent me to baptize in water, that one to me said, 'Upon whom ever you see the Spirit coming down and remaining upon him, this is the [one] baptizing in Spirit Holy.'

en.L: And I did not know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, but the one who sent me to baptize in water, that one said to me, 'The one on whom you see the Spirit coming down and remaining, this is the one who baptizes in [the] Holy Spirit.'
en.B: I myself did not know {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, but the one who sent me to baptize with water told me, 'When you see the Spirit come down and remain on someone, that is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'
en.R: I did not know who {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was. But God sent me to baptize people with water, and God told me, 'You will see the Spirit come down and remain on someone. That is the one who baptizes people with the Holy Spirit.'

decisions.choice: the one who sent me: God
decisions.reason: 1:6 said John was a man sent from God. His baptism was not his own idea: God gave it, and gave the sign that would show him the coming one.

decisions.choice: the sign is that the Spirit came down and remained
decisions.reason: "Remaining" repeats the verb of verse 32. The sign is not only that the Spirit came, but that the Spirit stayed on him.

decisions.choice: baptizes in the Holy Spirit: gives the Spirit to others
decisions.reason: The prophets promised that God would put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26-27; Joel 2:28). The one on whom the Spirit remains is the one who gives the Spirit; in John, Jesus gives the Spirit after he is glorified (7:39; 20:22). The present participle describes what he does, not one moment.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Readable names God, whom the phrase means (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: When you see ... on someone, that is the one
alternatives: The one on whom you see ..., this is the one
decisions.reason: English puts the condition first and avoids "on whom ... on him"; Literal keeps the Greek shape.

source.text: κἀγὼ ἑώρακα, καὶ μεμαρτύρηκα ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἐκλεκτὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And I have seen, and have testified that this is the chosen [one] of the God."

en.L: And I have seen, and I have testified that this one is the Chosen One of God."
en.B: I have seen it, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God."
en.R: I have seen this happen, and I am telling you that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is the one God has chosen."

decisions.choice: the Chosen One of God (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the chosen Son of God (a few early translations)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts, including the oldest papyri that contain this verse, read "the Son of God". "The Chosen One of God" is found in the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and in some of the earliest Latin and Syriac translations; a few combine the two. The SBLGNT prints "Chosen One" as the harder reading: a scribe was more likely to change an unusual title to the familiar "Son of God", which John uses often (1:49; 20:31), than the reverse. The evidence is divided, so a footnote gives "the Son of God". Either way the title marks Jesus as the one God has set apart, shown by the Spirit. Reviewers should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Chosen One: an echo of Isaiah 42:1
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 42:1 God speaks of "my chosen one, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him." That fits the sign John has just described. At the transfiguration the voice from the cloud says "This is my Son, my Chosen One" (Luke 9:35).

decisions.choice: two perfects: John's seeing and testifying stand on record
decisions.reason: Both verbs are perfect: what John saw and what he has declared remain as evidence. This closes the testimony that began in verse 19.

decisions.choice: the one God has chosen
decisions.reason: Readable says what the title means in plain words.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: Readable uses a pronoun for "this one", so it takes the deity_pronoun setting.

source.text: Τῇ ἐπαύριον πάλιν εἱστήκει ὁ Ἰωάννης καὶ ἐκ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ δύο, καὶ ἐμβλέψας τῷ Ἰησοῦ περιπατοῦντι λέγει· Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: On the next day again was standing the John and of the disciples of him two, \v 36 and having looked at the Jesus walking, he says, "Look, the lamb of the God."

en.L: On the next day again John was standing [there], and two of his disciples, \v 36 and looking at Jesus as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} walked by, he says, "Look, the Lamb of God!"
en.B: The next day John was there again with two of his disciples. \v 36 He watched Jesus walking by and said, "Look, there is the Lamb of God!"
en.R: The next day John was standing there again with two of his followers. \v 36 Jesus walked by. John looked at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and said, "Look! There is the Lamb of God!"

decisions.choice: disciples: learners who follow a teacher
decisions.reason: μαθητής is a pupil or follower. John the Baptist had disciples of his own (3:25; 4:1).

decisions.choice: looked intently
decisions.reason: ἐμβλέπω is a fixed, attentive look; the same verb is used in verse 42 of Jesus looking at Simon.

decisions.choice: the title of verse 29 again, now shorter
decisions.reason: John repeats "the Lamb of God" (see verse 29). This time his words send his own disciples after Jesus: the purpose of his testimony (1:7) begins to be fulfilled.

decisions.choice: followers
decisions.reason: Readable says what the word means; it uses "followers" through this passage.

decisions.choice: said
decisions.reason: Past tense, as in verse 21.

source.text: καὶ ἤκουσαν οἱ δύο μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος καὶ ἠκολούθησαν τῷ Ἰησοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And heard the two disciples him speaking, and they followed the Jesus.

en.L: And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus.
en.B: The two disciples heard what he said, and they followed Jesus.
en.R: The two followers heard what John said, and they began to follow Jesus.

decisions.choice: followed: walked after him, and so began to be his disciples
decisions.reason: ἀκολουθέω is the ordinary word for walking behind someone, and also John's word for being a disciple (1:43; 8:12; 21:19-22). Both senses are here: the two literally walk after Jesus, and this is where their discipleship begins.

decisions.choice: him speaking: John the Baptist
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to John, whose words they heard.

decisions.choice: follow
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "follow", which carries both senses (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: John
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker (meaning decision m2).

source.text: στραφεὶς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ θεασάμενος αὐτοὺς ἀκολουθοῦντας λέγει αὐτοῖς· Τί ζητεῖτε;

records.literal_gloss: Having turned and the Jesus and having beheld them following, he says to them, "What do you seek?"

en.L: Then Jesus, turning and seeing them following, says to them, "What are you seeking?"
en.B: Jesus turned and saw them following. He asked them, "What are you looking for?"
en.R: Jesus turned around and saw them following {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He asked them, "What do you want?"

decisions.choice: What are you seeking?: Jesus's first words in this Gospel
decisions.reason: The question is an ordinary one, but it is the first thing Jesus says in John, and it asks what the two really want. Jesus asks a like question of those who come to arrest him (18:4, 7) and of Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (20:15). ζητέω, to seek or look for, runs through the Gospel.

decisions.choice: What are you looking for? (B); What do you want? (R)
decisions.reason: Everyday English; Literal keeps "seeking", so the link with 20:15 can be seen.

source.text: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Ῥαββί ὃ λέγεται μεθερμηνευόμενον Διδάσκαλε, ποῦ μένεις;

records.literal_gloss: And they said to him, "Rabbi" (which is said, being translated, "Teacher"), "where are you staying?"

en.L: And they said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi" (which, translated, means Teacher), "where are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} staying?"
en.B: They answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi"—the word means Teacher—"where are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} staying?"
en.R: They said, "Rabbi" (this means Teacher), "where are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} staying?"

decisions.choice: Rabbi: a respectful title for a teacher, which John translates
decisions.reason: Ῥαββί is a Hebrew title, literally "my great one", used for teachers of the law. John explains it for readers who do not know Hebrew or Aramaic, as he does with Messiah (verse 41) and Cephas (verse 42). By using it the two treat Jesus as their teacher.

decisions.choice: staying: where he is lodging, with the deeper sense of remaining in view
decisions.reason: μένεις is the ordinary "stay, lodge": they ask where he is staying so they can spend time with him. But it is the same verb as the Spirit "remaining" on Jesus (verses 32-33), and later Jesus calls his disciples to "remain in me" (15:4-10). John uses an everyday word that opens onto the deeper one; the wish to be where Jesus stays is where that begins.

decisions.choice: staying
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: the natural word in its ordinary sense, with the note giving the link to "remain".

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: The deity_pronoun setting covers every pronoun for Christ: "you" when people speak to him and "me" or "my" when he speaks of himself, as well as "he" and "him". "I" is capitalized either way.

decisions.choice: which, translated, means
decisions.reason: Two Greek verbs ("is said", "being translated") make one English phrase.

source.text: λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ἔρχεσθε καὶ ὄψεσθε.

records.literal_gloss: He says to them, "Come, and you will see."

en.L: He says to them, "Come, and you will see."
en.B: He said to them, "Come, and you will see."
en.R: He told them, "Come and you will see."

decisions.choice: an invitation with a promise
decisions.reason: Jesus does not answer with an address. He invites them, and promises that they will see; the promise grows in verses 50-51, "you will see greater things". In John, seeing often leads on to understanding and believing.

decisions.choice: you will see (SBLGNT)
alternatives: see (a command, in many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts have the command "come and see", as in verse 46. The sense is nearly the same, so no footnote.

source.text: ἦλθαν οὖν καὶ εἶδαν ποῦ μένει, καὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ ἔμειναν τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην· ὥρα ἦν ὡς δεκάτη.

records.literal_gloss: They came therefore and saw where he stays, and with him they stayed the day that; [the] hour was about tenth.

en.L: So they came and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they stayed with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} that day; [the] hour was about [the] tenth.
en.B: So they went and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they spent the rest of that day with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. It was about four in the afternoon.
en.R: So they went and saw where {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was staying, and they stayed with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for the rest of that day. It was about four o'clock in the afternoon.

decisions.choice: the tenth hour: about four in the afternoon
alternatives: about ten in the morning, counting the hours from midnight
decisions.reason: Jews and most people of the time counted the hours of daylight from sunrise, about six in the morning, so the tenth hour was about four in the afternoon; Jesus speaks of "twelve hours in the day" (11:9). Some have argued that John counts from midnight, as Roman documents sometimes did, which would make it ten in the morning. A footnote gives the literal wording and the other way of counting.

decisions.choice: stayed: the same verb as "staying" in verse 38
decisions.reason: μένει and ἔμειναν repeat the verb of verse 38: they see where he stays, and they stay with him. See the note on verse 38 for the deeper sense of "remain".

decisions.choice: that day: for the rest of the day, perhaps also the night
decisions.reason: The phrase says how long they stayed. Since it was already late afternoon, they spent the rest of the day with him, and perhaps the night.

decisions.choice: about four in the afternoon
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: clock times stay literal at Literal, and Balanced and Readable give the modern time (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the rest of
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m3.

decisions.choice: went
decisions.reason: English tells the story from where the disciples were, so they "went".

source.text: ἦν Ἀνδρέας ὁ ἀδελφὸς Σίμωνος Πέτρου εἷς ἐκ τῶν δύο τῶν ἀκουσάντων παρὰ Ἰωάννου καὶ ἀκολουθησάντων αὐτῷ·

records.literal_gloss: Was Andrew the brother of Simon Peter one of the two of the [ones] having heard from John and having followed him;

en.L: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who heard from John and followed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, was one of the two who heard John's words and followed Jesus.
en.R: Andrew was one of the two who heard what John said and followed Jesus. Andrew was Simon Peter's brother.

decisions.choice: him: Jesus
decisions.reason: The two heard John and followed Jesus (verse 37).

decisions.choice: Simon Peter: the name readers know him by
decisions.reason: John calls him Simon Peter before Jesus gives him the name (verse 42), because his readers know him by it.

decisions.choice: the other of the two is not named
decisions.reason: John names Andrew but not the other disciple. Some have suggested it was the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is also never named (13:23), but this passage does not say.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1.

source.text: εὑρίσκει οὗτος πρῶτον τὸν ἀδελφὸν τὸν ἴδιον Σίμωνα καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Εὑρήκαμεν τὸν Μεσσίαν ὅ ἐστιν μεθερμηνευόμενον χριστός.

records.literal_gloss: Finds this one first the brother the own Simon and says to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which is, being translated, Christ).

en.L: He first finds his own brother Simon and says to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which is translated {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}).
en.B: The first thing Andrew did was to find his brother Simon and tell him, "We have found the Messiah" (that is, the {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}).
en.R: Andrew first went to find his brother Simon. He told him, "We have found the Messiah!" (Messiah is a Hebrew word for the {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}}, the king God promised.)

decisions.choice: Messiah: the Hebrew title, anointed one, which John translates
decisions.reason: Μεσσίαν is the Hebrew (and Aramaic) title written in Greek letters; John translates it with χριστός, the Greek word with the same meaning, "anointed". Kings (1 Samuel 16:13), priests and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil when God appointed them. By this time "the Anointed One" meant the king from David's line whom God had promised. Only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (here and 4:25).

decisions.choice: first (SBLGNT): the first thing he did
alternatives: he was the first to find (some manuscripts)
in the morning (a few early Latin manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have a form that makes Andrew the first of the two to find his brother; a few early Latin ones read "in the morning". The meaning changes only a little, so no footnote.

decisions.choice: We have found: the two disciples, and a discovery that holds
decisions.reason: "We" is Andrew and the other disciple. The perfect tense presents the finding as settled. Philip uses the same words in verse 45: each one who finds Jesus tells someone else.

decisions.choice: Messiah, plain; {{christos:Christ|Anointed One}} for the explanation
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for 1:41: Messiah is written plainly, since it is the word Andrew used. The christos setting is on the explanation only, and its alternative is "Anointed One", so no setting can produce "the Messiah (which means the Messiah)".

decisions.choice: Andrew
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Andrew for clarity.

decisions.choice: a Hebrew word for ... the king God promised
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the title meant (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἤγαγεν αὐτὸν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν.

records.literal_gloss: He led him to the Jesus.

en.L: He brought him to Jesus.
en.B: He brought Simon to Jesus.
en.R: Andrew brought Simon to Jesus.

decisions.choice: bringing others to Jesus
decisions.reason: Andrew does not argue; he brings his brother. The pattern repeats through the chapter (verse 45) and later (4:29; 12:22).

decisions.choice: Simon (B); Andrew, Simon (R)
decisions.reason: Names make plain who brought whom.

source.text: ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν· Σὺ εἶ Σίμων ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωάννου, σὺ κληθήσῃ Κηφᾶς ὃ ἑρμηνεύεται Πέτρος.

records.literal_gloss: Having looked at him the Jesus said, "You are Simon the son of John; you will be called Cephas" (which is translated Peter).

en.L: Jesus, looking at him, said, "You are Simon the son of John; you will be called Cephas" (which is translated Peter).
en.B: Jesus looked closely at him and said, "You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas" (which means Peter, that is, Rock).
en.R: Jesus looked straight at him and said, "You are Simon, son of John. But you will be called Cephas." (Cephas and Peter both mean Rock.)

decisions.choice: Cephas and Peter both mean rock
decisions.reason: Κηφᾶς is the Aramaic word for rock, written in Greek letters; Πέτρος is the Greek word for a rock or stone, used as a name. John translates one by the other. Paul usually calls him Cephas (1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9).

decisions.choice: you will be called: the new name looks ahead
decisions.reason: Jesus does not simply rename him; the future tense points to what Simon will become (compare Matthew 16:18). In Scripture God gives new names that mark a new calling, as with Abram and Jacob (Genesis 17:5; 32:28).

decisions.choice: son of John (SBLGNT)
alternatives: son of Jonah, or Jonas (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts read John here and in 21:15-17; many later ones read Jonah, as in Matthew 16:17 ("Bar-Jonah"). This John is not John the Baptist.

decisions.choice: looked closely
decisions.reason: The same fixed look as in verse 36.

decisions.choice: that is, Rock (B); both mean Rock (R)
decisions.reason: "Peter" is a translation only for those who know Greek; Balanced and Readable give the meaning (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: But
decisions.reason: Readable marks the contrast between his old name and the new one.

source.text: Τῇ ἐπαύριον ἠθέλησεν ἐξελθεῖν εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν.

records.literal_gloss: On the next day he wanted to go out into the Galilee.

en.L: On the next day [{{deity_pronoun:he|He}}] wanted to go out into Galilee.
en.B: The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee.
en.R: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee.

decisions.choice: the subject is Jesus
decisions.reason: The verb has no stated subject. The next sentence names Jesus as the one who calls Philip, and the story then moves north to Galilee (2:1).

decisions.choice: the days are counted
decisions.reason: John marks the days: the first day (1:19-28), the next day (1:29), the next day (1:35), the next day (here), and "on the third day" (2:1). Whether he means a week that echoes the week of creation, which his opening words recalled (1:1; Genesis 1:1), cannot be shown; at least the count ties the calling of the disciples to the first sign at Cana.

decisions.choice: [he] (L); Jesus (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs a subject (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: decided
decisions.reason: θέλω here is a decision to act, which he then carries out.

source.text: καὶ εὑρίσκει Φίλιππον καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀκολούθει μοι.

records.literal_gloss: And he finds Philip, and says to him the Jesus, "Follow me."

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} finds Philip, and Jesus says to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.B: He found Philip and said to him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.R: He found Philip and told him, "Follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Follow me: the call to be a disciple
decisions.reason: The present command asks for continuing to follow. It is the same verb as in verse 37; here Jesus himself gives the call. The others in this chapter are brought by someone else.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 38: the setting covers every pronoun for Christ.

source.text: ἦν δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδά, ἐκ τῆς πόλεως Ἀνδρέου καὶ Πέτρου.

records.literal_gloss: Was now the Philip from Bethsaida, out of the city of Andrew and Peter.

en.L: Now Philip was from Bethsaida, from the town of Andrew and Peter.
en.B: Philip came from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter.
en.R: Philip was from the town of Bethsaida. Andrew and Peter came from there too.

decisions.choice: city: a town of any size
decisions.reason: πόλις is any town with its own community. Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

decisions.choice: where they came from, not necessarily where they lived
decisions.reason: Mark 1:21, 29 places the house of Simon and Andrew in Capernaum, a few miles away. Bethsaida is the town they came from.

source.text: εὑρίσκει Φίλιππος τὸν Ναθαναὴλ καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Ὃν ἔγραψεν Μωϋσῆς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ καὶ οἱ προφῆται εὑρήκαμεν, Ἰησοῦν υἱὸν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρέτ.

records.literal_gloss: Finds Philip the Nathanael and says to him, "[The one] whom wrote Moses in the law and the prophets we have found, Jesus son of the Joseph, the [one] from Nazareth."

en.L: Philip finds Nathanael and says to him, "The one about whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets [also], we have found: Jesus, son of Joseph, the one from Nazareth."
en.B: Philip found Nathanael and told him, "Moses wrote about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the law, and so did the prophets, and now we have found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth."
en.R: Then Philip found Nathanael and told him, "Moses wrote about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the law, and the prophets did too. Now we have found {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}! His name is Jesus. He is the son of Joseph, from Nazareth."

decisions.choice: Moses in the law and the prophets: the Scriptures of Israel
decisions.reason: "Moses in the law and the prophets" names the Scriptures by two of their main parts (compare Luke 24:27, 44). Moses wrote of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15, 18; see verse 21), and the prophets spoke of the coming king. Philip believes Jesus is the one they point to; Jesus says the same of the Scriptures in 5:39, 46.

decisions.choice: son of Joseph, from Nazareth: how people knew him
decisions.reason: This is how Jesus was ordinarily identified: by his father's name and his town (compare 6:42). John does not correct Philip. His readers already know from 1:1-14 where Jesus really comes from, and the question of his origin returns in 7:27-28 and 7:41-42.

decisions.choice: Moses wrote about him ... now we have found him
alternatives: We have found the one Moses wrote about ...
decisions.reason: The Greek puts the one Moses wrote about first and "we have found" late, building up to the name. Balanced and Readable keep that order by saying "him" twice.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The pronouns refer to Jesus.

source.text: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Ἐκ Ναζαρὲτ δύναταί τι ἀγαθὸν εἶναι;

records.literal_gloss: And said to him Nathanael, "Out of Nazareth can something good be?"

en.L: And Nathanael said to him, "Out of Nazareth can anything good be?"
en.B: Nathanael answered, "Can anything good be from a place like Nazareth?"
en.R: Nathanael said, "Nazareth? Does anything good ever come from that town?"

decisions.choice: Nazareth was small and unimportant
decisions.reason: Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, never named in the Old Testament, and no one looked for the Messiah to come from it (compare 7:41-42, 52). Nathanael himself came from Cana (21:2), another town of Galilee.

decisions.choice: a doubting question
decisions.reason: The words alone do not show what answer is expected, but Nathanael's tone is doubtful: he cannot believe that anyone important could come from Nazareth.

decisions.choice: a place like
decisions.reason: Shows the doubt of meaning decision m2 in natural English.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Φίλιππος· Ἔρχου καὶ ἴδε.

records.literal_gloss: Says to him the Philip, "Come and see."

en.L: Philip says to him, "Come and see."
en.B: Philip said to him, "Come and see."
en.R: Philip answered, "Come and see for yourself."

decisions.choice: Come and see: the invitation Jesus gave
decisions.reason: Philip answers doubt the way Jesus answered the first two disciples (verse 39): not with an argument, but with an invitation to come and see.

decisions.choice: for yourself
decisions.reason: The command is to see in person; Readable says so.

source.text: εἶδεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν Ναθαναὴλ ἐρχόμενον πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ λέγει περὶ αὐτοῦ· Ἴδε ἀληθῶς Ἰσραηλίτης ἐν ᾧ δόλος οὐκ ἔστιν.

records.literal_gloss: Saw the Jesus the Nathanael coming toward him and says about him, "Look, truly an Israelite in whom deceit not is."

en.L: Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and says about him, "Look, truly an Israelite, in whom deceit is not!"
en.B: When Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said of him, "Here is a true Israelite: there is nothing deceitful in him."
en.R: Jesus saw Nathanael coming. He said, "Here comes a real Israelite! There is nothing false about him."

decisions.choice: an echo of Jacob, the man of deceit who was renamed Israel
decisions.reason: Isaac told Esau that Jacob had come "with deceit" and taken his blessing (Genesis 27:35), and the Greek translation of that verse uses this same word, δόλος. Later God renamed Jacob "Israel" (Genesis 32:28). Nathanael is an Israelite without the deceit of Jacob; verse 51 goes on to recall Jacob's dream. Psalm 32:2 blesses the one "in whose spirit there is no deceit".

decisions.choice: truly an Israelite: a true Israelite, worthy of the name
decisions.reason: ἀληθῶς qualifies "Israelite": Nathanael is what an Israelite should be (compare Romans 9:6).

decisions.choice: deceit: trickery, falseness
decisions.reason: δόλος is cunning or trickery. Nathanael's blunt question in verse 46 already showed that he says what he thinks.

decisions.choice: Here is (B); Here comes (R)
decisions.reason: Natural English for pointing someone out as he approaches.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: These pronouns refer to Jesus; "him" in "said of him" is Nathanael and has no setting.

source.text: λέγει αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Πόθεν με γινώσκεις;

records.literal_gloss: Says to him Nathanael, "From where me do you know?"

en.L: Nathanael says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "From where do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"
en.B: Nathanael asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "How do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"
en.R: Nathanael asked, "How do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} know me?"

decisions.choice: From where?: how is it that?
decisions.reason: Πόθεν literally asks "from where", and can also mean "how is it that" (as in Mark 12:37). The same word asks where Jesus himself is from (7:27; 9:29; 19:9).

decisions.choice: How
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Πρὸ τοῦ σε Φίλιππον φωνῆσαι ὄντα ὑπὸ τὴν συκῆν εἶδόν σε.

records.literal_gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "Before the you Philip to call, being under the fig tree, I saw you."

en.L: Jesus answered and said to him, "Before Philip called you, being under the fig tree, I saw you."
en.B: Jesus answered, "I saw you while you were still under the fig tree, before Philip called you."
en.R: Jesus answered, "I saw you under the fig tree, even before Philip called you."

decisions.choice: being: Nathanael was the one under the fig tree
alternatives: Jesus was under the fig tree
decisions.reason: ὄντα agrees with "you": Nathanael was under the tree.

decisions.choice: Jesus knew what he could not have seen in an ordinary way
decisions.reason: Jesus saw Nathanael where no one could have told him, and Nathanael takes it as a sign of who Jesus is (verse 49). John notes elsewhere that Jesus knew what was in people (2:24-25; 4:17-18).

decisions.choice: the fig tree: an ordinary place of shade, with a picture of peace behind it
decisions.reason: John does not say what Nathanael was doing there. A fig tree gave shade near a house, and "each under his vine and under his fig tree" was a picture of peace in Israel (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). The translation leaves the image as it stands.

decisions.choice: I saw you ... before Philip called you
alternatives: Before Philip called you ... I saw you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable lead with the main statement; Literal keeps the Greek order.

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ Ναθαναήλ· Ῥαββί, σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, σὺ βασιλεὺς εἶ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ.

records.literal_gloss: Answered him Nathanael, "Rabbi, you are the son of the God, you king are of the Israel."

en.L: Nathanael answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are King of Israel."
en.B: Nathanael answered, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are Israel's King!"
en.R: Nathanael answered, "Rabbi, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God! You are the promised King of Israel!"

decisions.choice: Son of God: here a royal title for the Messiah, which the Gospel fills out
decisions.reason: Paired with "King of Israel", "Son of God" recalls God's promise to David's heir, "I will be his father, and he will be my son" (2 Samuel 7:14), and Psalm 2, where God calls his anointed king his son (Psalm 2:6-7). Nathanael means at least that Jesus is the promised king. John's readers already know that the Son is far more (1:14, 18), and the book is written so that they may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31).

decisions.choice: King of Israel: the promised king
decisions.reason: Zephaniah 3:15 calls the LORD himself the King of Israel in the midst of his people. The crowd greets Jesus with this title when he enters Jerusalem (12:13), and the notice on the cross calls him "King of the Jews" (19:19).

decisions.choice: King without the article: still definite
decisions.reason: The noun comes before the verb without the article, a common way to make such a predicate definite: Nathanael means the King, not one king among others.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 38. At the start of a sentence "You" is written plain.

decisions.choice: promised
decisions.reason: Readable says what the title means here (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ὅτι εἶπόν σοι ὅτι εἶδόν σε ὑποκάτω τῆς συκῆς πιστεύεις;

records.literal_gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "Because I said to you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe?

en.L: Jesus answered and said to him, "Because I said to you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe?
en.B: Jesus replied, "Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree?
en.R: Jesus answered, "Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree?

decisions.choice: a question (SBLGNT)
alternatives: a statement: you believe because I told you
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts have no question marks, so it could be read either way. Either way Jesus is not rejecting Nathanael's faith: he accepts it and promises more (the next sentence).

decisions.choice: believe: real faith, at its beginning
decisions.reason: Key term. After the opening (1:7, 12), this is the first time in the story that someone is said to believe. Jesus accepts it, and promises that what Nathanael has seen is small next to what is coming.

decisions.choice: Do you believe because ...?
decisions.reason: Natural English order for the question.

decisions.choice: just
decisions.reason: The contrast with "greater things" in the next sentence implies it.

source.text: μείζω τούτων ὄψῃ.

records.literal_gloss: Greater things than these you will see."

en.L: Greater things than these you will see."
en.B: You will see greater things than that."
en.R: You will see greater things than this."

decisions.choice: greater things: what Jesus will do and show
decisions.reason: The plural looks ahead to the signs that begin at Cana (2:11) and to what the next sentence describes. The verb is singular, spoken to Nathanael; the next sentence widens the promise to all.

decisions.choice: than that (B); than this (R)
decisions.reason: English refers to one event with a singular word.

source.text: καὶ λέγει αὐτῷ· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.

records.literal_gloss: And he says to him, "Amen, amen, I say to you, you will see the heaven having been opened and the angels of the God going up and coming down upon the son of the man."

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to him, "Truly, truly I say to you [all], you will see the heaven standing open and the angels of God going up and coming down upon the Son of Man."
en.B: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him, "Truly, truly, I tell you all: you will see heaven standing open, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man."
en.R: Then Jesus said, "I tell you the truth: all of you will see heaven open wide, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man."

decisions.choice: Amen, amen: a solemn pledge that what follows is true
decisions.reason: Ἀμὴν is a Hebrew word meaning "it is sure". People normally said it in response to someone else's prayer or oath (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; Nehemiah 8:6). Jesus puts it before his own words, as a pledge of their truth. Only in John is it doubled, twenty-five times; this is the first.

decisions.choice: you: plural, addressed to more than Nathanael
decisions.reason: "He says to him" is singular, but ὑμῖν and ὄψεσθε are plural: the promise is for all the disciples.

decisions.choice: Jacob's dream at Bethel (Genesis 28:12)
decisions.reason: Jacob dreamed of a stairway set on the earth and reaching to heaven, with the angels of God going up and coming down on it (Genesis 28:12); the words here follow the Greek of that verse closely. Jacob called the place the house of God and the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:17). Jesus says that he himself is where heaven and earth meet: the angels go up and down on the Son of Man. Together with the echo of Jacob in verse 47, the promise is that Nathanael will see more than Jacob saw.

decisions.choice: heaven opened and standing open
decisions.reason: The perfect participle says heaven has been opened and stays open: the way between God and people is open, as when heaven opened in the visions of the prophets (Ezekiel 1:1) and at Jesus's baptism (Mark 1:10).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus's name for himself, recalling Daniel 7:13-14
alternatives: a son of man: simply a human being
decisions.reason: In Hebrew "son of man" can mean simply a human being (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). In Daniel 7:13-14 one "like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule from God. In the Gospels Jesus uses the title of himself, and others only repeat it (12:34). In John the Son of Man has come down from heaven and will be lifted up (3:13-14). Nathanael has called him Son of God and King; Jesus answers with the title he chooses for himself.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John, recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: [all] (L); you all (B); all of you (R)
decisions.reason: English "you" does not show the plural (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man, with capitals and no gender setting
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John: a title, so it is never under the gender setting.

decisions.choice: going up and coming down
decisions.reason: Plain English verbs at every level; the note gives the link to Genesis 28:12.
